OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon'ble Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Ashis Sen and Shri Banarsi Das Gupta, former Members of 
this House. 
Shri Ashis Sen passed away on the 24th August, 2007, at the age of 85 years. 
Born at Hooghly district of West Bengal in November 1922, Shri Sen had his 
education at Scottish Church College and Vidyasagar College, Kolkata. 
A trade unionist, Shri Sen was associated with various Banking Employ ees' 
Associations in different capacities and suffered imprisonment for his trade union 
activities in 1956. He also served as President of the All India Regional Rural Banks 
Employees' Association. Shri Sen wrote articles on economic issues and trade 
union movement in newspapers and periodicals and was also Editor of the Trade 
Union Journal from 1949 to 1960. 
Shri Sen represented the State of West Bengal in this House from April, 1988 to 
April, 1994. In the passing away of Shri Ashis Sen, the country has lo st a noted 
trade unionist. 
Shri Banarsi Das Gupta passed away on the 29th August, 2007 at the age of 90 
years. Bom at Manheru in the Bhiwani district of Haryana in November 1917, 
Shri Gupta had his education at the Birla Inter College, Pilani. 
       A social worker, Shri Gupta was associated with various social welfare and  
ucational organizations. He worked for the uplift of Harijans and backward  sses 
and for spreading education, particularly in rural  areas.  He waged a  uggle 
against the practice of untou chability, dowry and child marriage and stood 
GOwidow remarriage.  Shri  Gupta participated in  the freedom  struggle and   
tablished Praja Mandal in the erstwhile Jind State in the pre -Independence eriod.  
He  was  imprisoned  several  times  for  launchin g  an  agitation  for  
establishment of a responsible Government there 
A true follower of Acharya Vinoba Bhave, Shri Gupta undertook several 
padyatras and collected thousands ef acres of land for distribution among the 
landless during the Bhoodan Movement. Shri Gupta also edited Hindi weekly Apna 
Desh and Haryana Kesri for many years. 

2      Obituary [RAJYA SABHA] References 
The legislative career of Shri Gupta started with the membership of the Haryana 
Legislative Assembly, where he was a Member three times. He was also Speaker of that State 
Assembly. He served as Minister in the Government of Haryana for several years and 
had the distinction of serving as Chief Minister of that State twice. Shri Gupta 
represented the State of Haryana in this House from April, 1996 to April, 2002. 
In the passing away of Shri Gupta, the country has lost an able Parliamentarian, an 
efficient Administrator and a dedicated social worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Ashis Sen and Shri Banarsi Das Gupta.  
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect to 
the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR.CHAIRMAN: Secretary-Genieral will convey to the members of the bereaved  
family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

Unemployment in textile sector due to appreciation of rupee against dollar 
*301. DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA:     
SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN†† 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per the report of Confederation of Indian Textile Industry 
about 6 lakh people will be rendered jobless due to adverse effect of appreciation of rupee 
against dollar on exports; 
(b) if so, how many people directly associated with textile trade are likely to be affected; 
(c) whether Government have envisaged any plan to see that such huge labour force 
engaged in direct and indirect textile trade is not adversely affected; and 
(d) if so, among those affected labour, how many are associated with handloom 
business in the country? 
• 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) to (d) A  
Statement is laid on the Table of the House.   
Statement 
(a) to (b) The Report of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI) indicates 
that stagnation of exports in 2007-08 due to unprecedented appreciation

employment in the textiles and clothing industry will be to the tune of 2.72 lakh.. 
(c) The Report of the CITI his not quantified the existing job loss. However,  
the Government has taken following steps to mitigate the deceleration of exports  
on account of Rupee appreciation:

Projects under NREGA 
*303. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of completed pr ojects under National Rural Employment 
Guarantee Act (NREGA) in different States and Union Territories for the year 2006 -
2007; 
(b) whether Government are contemplating to enhance the rates of wages for 
NREGA works in the context of price-rise; 
(c) whether Governme nt have made any assessment on the output of the works so 
far completed; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) State-wise details of works along with percentage of completed works during 
2006-07 is given in Statement -I (See below). Incomplete works of 2006- 07 have been 
continued in 2007-08. 
(b) No, Sir. Section 6(1) of the NREG Act provides that the Central Government 
may, by notification, specify the wage rate for the purposes of the Act. Section 6(2) 
further provides that until such time a wage rate is fixed by the Central Government in 
respect of any area in a State, the minimum wage fixed by the State under Section 3 of 
the Minimum Wages Act 1948 for agricultural labourers shall be considered as the wage 
rate applicable to that area. Central Government has not fixed a wage rate under 
NREGA for any of the States. Therefore, the minimum wages notified for agricultural 
labourers under M inimum Wages Act by the State Governments are applicable to 
NREGA. 
(c) and (d) Assessment on the output of projects under NREGA is being done by the 
Government. Village level Monitoring and Vigilance Committees have been set up to 
certify the completion of works under the Act. National Level Monitors 

Oral Answers [5 SEP., 2007] to Questions      9 
(NLMs) have made 219 visits to the 200 phase-I districts and have also visited 113 phase-II 
districts in which NREGA has been implemented with effect from 1.4.2007. Instructions have 
been issued to States for inspection of 2% of works at State level, 10% works at District 
level and 100% works at Block level. Section 17(2) of the Act provides that the Gram Sabha 
shall conduct regular social audit of all the projects  taken up within the Gram Panchayat. 
Members of the Central Employment Guarantee Council have participated in the Social Audit 
of projects conducted in Jharkhand and Tamil Nadu. Instructions have been issued to all 
the States to complete Social Audit of all the projects within three months.

Functioning of jails 
*314. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the functioning of jails in the country has not improved despite the 
recommendations given by various Reforms Commissions and Committees; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor;   
(c) the number of deaths/suicides occurred in jails during the last three years; and 
(d) the number of undertrials for over ten years in jails and those without trial for over 
two years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) and (b) "Prisons" is a state subject under List II of the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution of India and, therefore, functioning of jails comes under the 
realm of the respective State Governments. Committees set up to look into issues relating to 
prison reforms and correctional administration have made several recommendations to 
improve the functioning and condition in prisons. Most of these recommendations 
primarily focused on tightening of security in prisons, improving the physical cond itions 
and providing basic amenities to prisoners. Emphasis was also laid on vocational 
rehabilitative programmes with a view to integrate prisoners into society once they 
complete their sentence. 
The Central Government has also taken the following measure s to supplement the 
efforts of the State Governments in this regard:- 
(1) The Government of India is implementing the Scheme for Modernization of 
Prisons to reduce overcrowding and improving the condition in prisons. The 
components of the Scheme include constr uction of new jails, repair and 
renovation of existing jails, improvement in sanitation and water supply and 
construction of staff quarters for prison personnel. 
(2) Advisories have been issued to the State Governments for strengthening 
security in jails. ' 
(3) The Government of India had prepared a Model Prison Manual which was 
circulated to all the State Governments/ Union Territories for their guidance. 
The manual aims at bringing in basic uniformity in laws, rules and 
regulations governing every aspect of prison administration and management. 
(4) With a view to provide relief to undertrial prisoners, a new section viz. 436A of 
the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has been inserted in the Code to provide 
that where an undertrial prisoner other than the one

Supply of pure drinking water 
 †*315. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether consumption of polluted and fluoride containing water causes  
serious diseases affecting health; 
(b) whether people living in a number of rural areas of the country are forced to consume 
such water; 
(c) if so, whether Government have formulated any permanent scheme to provide 
pure and potable water across the nation in order to protect people from such serious 
diseases; 
(d) if so, the details regarding nature of said scheme; and  
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): 
(a) Consumption of water containing fluoride in excess of the prescribed limit of 1.5 mg/litre 
is harmful to human health. Pollutants, both chemical and bacteriological, are harmful, if 
found to be in excess of the prescribed safety limits. 
(b) to (e) The Government of India have two major programmes to address water 
quality problems and to provide access to safe drinking water to the rural communities. 
(i) Under the Sub -Mission on Water Qual ity program, financial and technical 
assistance is provided for tackling specific chemical quality problems like 
arsenic, fluoride, nitrate, iron, salinity and multiple problems in the affected 
areas. Technical assistance and advice is given to State Gover nments on 
appropriate treatment technologies, safe alternate sources and utilization of 
recharge/water harvesting and other methods of mitigating quality problems in 
rural drinking water supply. Financial assistance is provided by the 
Government of India o n duly approved projects with funding pattern of 
75:25 basis between Centre and State. In the year 2006-07, Rs. 735.67 crore 
was provided as Central share for taking up such projects to provide safe 
potable water in the affected areas. During the current financial year 2007-08, an 
amount of Rs.1,300 crore has been allocated under this programme. It is 
proposed to address the problems of all water quality affected habitations in the 
country under Bharat Nirman programme before 2009. 
(ii) The National Rural D rinking Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance 
Programme under which assistance is provid"d to States

for testing of all drinking water s ources in the rural areas by the  
community using simple to use field test kits to act as early warning  
system. Awareness generation about water quality issues and its  
impact on health, training and capacity building of rural communities  
for conducting wate r testing and sanitary surveys are major  
components of the Programme. During 2005- 06 and 2006- 07, funds to

Confusing parameters for census of BPL 
t*318. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that parameters for census of people living below poverty line 
vary, causing confusion; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that problem has become more serious due to non-uniformity 
in the parameters of Central Government and State Governments; 
(c) whether Government are considering to set up a task force in this regard; and 
(d) if not, the State -wise number of poor persons and the details of the parameters 
adopted for their identification? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): 
(a) to (d) The Ministry of Ru ral Development conducts the BPL Census generally in the 
beginning of the Five Year Plan to identify the rural households living Below the Poverty 
Line who could be assisted under its various programmes. The BPL Census was conducted 
earlier in 1992 for the Eighth Five Year Plan and in 1997 for the Ninth Five Year Plan using 
the income and expenditure criteria respectively. For the Tenth Five Year Plan, BPL Census 
2002 has been conducted using the uniform methodology of 'Score Based Ranking' of the 
rural households 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

Written Answers to [5 SEP., 2007] Starred Questions     31 
for which 13 socio- economic parameters have been used. This methodology was 
recommended by the Expert Group constituted by the Mini stry and was adopted after a 
wide range of discussions with different stakeholders including the State Governments 
which is considered to be an improvement over the methodologies based on income and 
expenditure approach used for the previous BPL Censuses. However, some of the States 
like Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and West Bengal have conducted more comprehensive 
surveys to meet their own State specific requirements of statistics, but it has been 
promised to furnish the BPL list to this Ministry on the basis of  prescribed 
methodology. 
The results of BPL Census 2002 could not be finalized as was stipulated  
originally because of the stay order passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court on 
5.5.2003 during the hearing of a Writ Petition No. 196 of 2001 in the matter of PUC L 
Vs. Union of India. The stay was vacated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court on  
14.2.2006. Immediately after vacation of the stay, the State Governments were 
advised to finalise the BPL list in a transparent manner by taking the measures of  
giving wide publicit y, to get the approval of the Gram Sabha, displaying the list at  
the Panchayat Headquarters, to keep the printed copies in the booklet form at the  
Panchayat Headquarters and paint the list of BPL households on the wall of the  
Panchayat Building in the asce nding order along with posting it on the website. A  
two-stage appeal mechanism was also introduced to redress the public grievances.  
The State Governments are reported to have received a large number of objections  
which took considerable time to resolve th em. A number of States are still in the  
process of finalizing the BPL list and there is no proposal at present to set up any  
Task Force.   
Under the guidelines of BPL Census 2002, the States were given the option to 
identify the number of BPL households in  the rural areas in such a way that it should be 
equal to the poverty estimates of 1999- 2000 or the Adjusted Share worked out by the 
Planning Commission, whichever is higher. Another 10% flexibility was allowed to 
account for the transient poor. The number  of BPL households on the basis of Adjusted 
Share and poverty estimates of 1999- 2000 is at Statement -I {See below). A Statement 
indicating the list of States who have finalized the BPL list on the basis of BPL Census 
2002 along with the total number of rur al BPL households identified is at Statement -II 
(See below). The list of parameters prescribed for BPL Census 2002 is at Statement-Ill.

Impact of liberalized import 
*319. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted any study to assess the impact of liberalized 
import under various regional and bilateral trade agreements, o f agricultural products on 
Indian agriculture; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the protection given to Indian farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL NATH): (a) and 
(b) Before entering into any negotiation for a bilateral or regional Free Trade Agreement, 
studies are undertaken internally, as well as through joint study groups to examine the 
feasibility of the proposed agreement, including its impact on the domestic agriculture and 
industrial sectors. TVpically, the Free Trade Agreemen ts protect sensitive products of the 
two sides through the inclusion of negative lists as well as a safeguards mechanism to 
protect against possible surges in imports. The Government, in close consultation with the 
concerned Ministries, decides on the agricultural products that need to be included in the 
negative list of a particular agreement, where no tariff concessions are to be offered. A 
reduction in customs duties is offered in respect of certain agricultural products only after 
taking into account the sensitivities of our agricultural sector and the potential volume of 
trade in these products.

Statement   
     Details regarding terms of reference of the Commission 
The terms of reference of the Commission on Centre-State Relations, which has been set 
up under the Chairpersonship of Shri Justice Madan Mohan Punchhi (Retd.), former 
Chief Justice of India, are as follows: 
(i) The Commission will examine and review the working of the existing arrangements 
between the Union and States as per the Constitution of India, the healthy 
precedents being followed, various pronouncements • of the Courts in regard to 
powers, functions and responsibilities in all spheres including legislative relations, 
administrative relations, role of governors, emergency provisions, financial 
relations, economic and social planning, Panchayati Raj institutions, sharing of 
resources; including inter-State river water and recommend such changes or other 
measures as may be appropriate keeping in view the practical difficulties. 
(ii) In examining and reviewing the working of the existing arrangements between 
the Union and States and making recommendations as to the changes and 
measures needed, the Commission will keep in view the social and economic 
developments that have taken place over the years particularly over the last two 
decades and have due regard to the scheme and framework of the Constitution. 
Such recommendations would also need to address the growing challenges of 
ensuring good governance for promoting the welfare of the people whilst 
strengthening the unity and integrity of the country, and of availing emerging 
opportunities for sustained and rapid economic growth for alleviating poverty 
and illiteracy in the early decades of the new  millennium. 
(iii) While examining and making its recommendations on the above, the Commission 
shall have particular regard, but not limit its mandate to the foUowing:- 
(a) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre vis-a-vis States 
during major and prolonged outbreaks of communal violence, caste violence 
or any other social conflict leading to prolonged and escalated violence. 

Written Answers to [5 AUG, 2007] Unstarred Questions    87 
(b) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre vis-a-vis States in 
the planning and implementation of the mega projects like' the inter-
linking of rivers, that would normally take 15-20 years for completion and 
hinge vitally on the support of the States. 
(c) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre vis-a-vis States in 
promoting effective devolution of powers and autonomy to Panchayati Raj 
Institutions and Local Bodies including the Autonomous Bodies under the 
6 Schedule of the Constitution within a specified period of time. 
(d) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre vis-a-vis States in 
promoting the concept and practice of independent planning and budgeting at 
the District level. 
(e) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre vis-a.-vis States in 
linking Cen tral assistance of various kinds with the performance of the 
States. 
(f) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre in adopting 
approaches and policies based on positive discrimination in favour of backward 
States. 
(g) The impact of the recommenda tions made by the 8th to 12th  
Finance Commissions on the fiscal relations between the Centre and  
the States, especially the greater dependence of the States on  
devolution of funds from the Centre. 
(h) The need and relevance of separate taxes on the product ion and on the 
sales of goods and services subsequent to the introduction of Value Added 
Tax regime. 
(i) The need for freeing inter-State trade in order to establish a unified and 
integrated domestic market as also in the context of the reluctance of State 
Governments to adopt the relevant Sarkaria Commission's recommendation 
in chapter XVIII of its report. 
(j) The need for setting up a Central Law Enforcement Agency empowered 
to take up suo moto investigation of crimes having inter -State and/or 
international ramifications with serious implications on national security. 
(k) The feasibility of a supporting legislation under Article 355 for the purpose 
of suo moto deployment of Central forces in the States if and when the 
situation so demands.

as 300 per cent and inmates sleep in shifts; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that the overwhelming majority of those incarcerated are 
poor, dalits, adivasis and minorities; and 
(e) if so, what Government propose to do in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) and (b) A s per statistics compiled by the National Crime 
Records Bureau, there were 237076 undertrials detained in various jails of the country 
as on 31.12.2005. The State -wise details of undertrials imprisoned under different 
offences of Indian Penal Code (IPC), S pecial Local Laws and Civil cases are at

(c) The capacity of different jails in the country, population of inmates kept in them 
and occupancy rate therein as on 31.12.2005 is at Statement (See below). 
(d) The Religion and Caste wise break up of inmates kept in jails at the end of 2005 
is at Statement-V (See below). 
(e) "Prisons" is a state subject under List II of the Seventh Schedule to the 
Constitution of India and Prison Administration is primarily the responsibility  of the 
respective State Governments. However, with a view to supplement the efforts of the 
State Governments, the following reform measures have been taken up by the Central 
Government: 
1.    In order to improve the condition of prisons, prisoners and the  prison staff, 
the Central Government launched a non -plan scheme in 2002- 03 for 
construction of additional prisons to reduce overcrowding, repair and 
renovation of existing prisons, improvement in sanitation and water supply 
and living accommodation for pr ison staff. The scheme is being 
implemented over a period of five years with an outlay of Rs. 1800 crore 
on cost sharing basis in the ratio of 75:25 between the Central and State 
Governments respectively. 
2     A new section viz 436 of the Code of Criminal  Procedure, 1973 has been 
inserted in the Code to provide that where an undertrial prisoner other than 
the one accused of an offence for which death has been prescribed as one 
of the punishments, has been under detention for a period extending to one -
half of the maximum period of imprisonment, provided for the alleged 
offence, he should be released on his personal bond, with or without 
sureties. It also provides that, in no case will an undertrail prisoner be 
detained beyond the maximum period of imprisonme nt for which he can be 
convicted for the alleged offence. 
Section 436 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has also been 
amended to make a mandatory provision that if the arrested person is 
accused for a bailable offence and he is an indigent and cannot furnish 
surety, the Court shall release him on his execution of a bond without 
sureties.

 basic  uniformity  in  laws,  rules  and regulations  governing  the  
dministration of prisons and the management of prisoners all over the country; 
       rationalization of prison practices to cater effectively to various categori es 
of prisoners, spelling out minimum standards of  institutional services for tbe

Rate of interest on EPF 
2409. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that no decision was taken on the rate of interest payable on 
deposits in EPF during the course of the meeting of EPF Board held in March, 2007; ' 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether Government would take a long term view on this question, when the economic 
position of the country is quite sound? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The matter regarding 
rate of interest for the year 2006 -07 was placed before the Central Board of Trustees, 
Employees' Provident Fund in its 179th meeting held on 10.03.2007. However, the matter was 
deferred as it required more discussions at various levels. Subsequently, the Board in its special 
meeting held on 23.07.2007 recommended the rate of interest for the year 2006-07 as 8.5%. 
(c) As per the provisions of the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme 1952, interest is 
required to be credited to the account of each member at such ra te as may be determined 
by the Central Government in consultation with the Central Board of Trustees. The rate of 
interest to be credited on EPF accounts in any particular year is determined in such a 
manner that there should be no overdrawal on the Interest Suspense Account as a result 
of debit thereto of the interest credited to members' accounts.

Protection of services to workers in unorganised sector 
2412. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of workers engaged in the unorganised sector; 
(b) how many of them belong to agri and non-agri sector; 

136  Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions 
(c) in how many cases there is no means of protection of their services; and 
(d) whether Government propose to frame rules and take steps to give  
protection and do justice in respect of services of these workers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) and (b) According to the survey conducted 
by the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) during 2004-05, the total number of 
workers in the unorganized sector was 43.3 crores. Out of which, about' 26.8 crore are in the 
agriculture sector and remaining in the non-agriculture sector. 
(c) and (d) The Government has initiated several measures for the protection of the 
labourers in the unorganised sector. Various labour laws like the Minimum Wages Act, 1948; 
the Workmen Compensation Act, 1923; the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976; the Building 
and other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) 
Act, 1996, Contract L abour (Abolition and Prohibtion) Act, 1970, Inter -State Migrant 
Workmen (RECS) Act, 1979 etc. are applicable to the labourers in the unorganized sector 
also. The Government have set up Welfare Funds to provide social security/welfare 
measures to certain categories of workers i.e. beedi workers, certain non-coal mine workers 
and cine workers. The welfare measures include health care, housing, educational 
assistance for children, drinking water supply, etc. Further, the Janshree Bima Yojana 
provides life insu rance protection to the rural and urban poor persons, including 
unorganized workers who are below and marginally above the poverty line. In addition to 
this, the Government is also implementing various welfare and employment oriented 
schemes and programmes through various Ministries/ Departments. The Government has 
recently enacted National Rural Employment Guarantee Act which provides 100 days of 
guaranteed wage employment in every financial year to every household whose adult 
members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. The Government propose to enact The 
Unorganised Sector Workers Social Security Bill with a view to providing social security to 
unorganized sector workers.

2418. SHRI A. VUAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are many Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) 
schemes in Kerala undertaken with the assistance of Central Government;

as on today, categorj'-wise;

of the scheme within three years;   
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) The primary responsibility of providing drinking 
water in rural area rests 'vith the State Governroenis. The Government of India supplements 
efforts made by the States by providing financial and technical assistance under a centrally 
sponsored programme, namely Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). 
The allocation under ARW SP is based on well -defined parameters viz. rural population, 
geographical conditions, number of Not Covered (NC)/Partially Covered (PC) habitations 
and water quality status. However, State Governments are empowered to plan, sanction and 
implement drinking water schemes. Therefore, scheme wise details/records for ARWSP are 
maintained by respective States at their level. 
(c) to (e) The total central allocation for the State under ARWSP for 2007-08 is Rs. 86.56 
crore. A request was received from Managing Director, Kerala Water Works Authority for 
reimbursement of Rs. 713.58 lakh for excess expenditure incurred during 2004 -05 and 
2005-06. Since guidelines do not provide for reimbursement of excess expenditure, the 
Slate Government was informed accordingly. The State Government was requested to 
submit proposal for release of additional funds, which can be considered after reviewing 
physical/financial

2419. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA:   
   SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that Prime Minister while inaugurating Two day annual 
conference on rural water supply and sanitation warned about severe water shortage in 
the next few decades and advocated collective action by all State Governments to 
empower district level institutional structures to handle water supply, fund water 
recharge activities through NREGA and capacity building of health engineering 
departments in geo-hydrology so that they are able to appreciate issue of environmental 
sustainability; 
(b) the decision taken in the conference; and   
(c) the steps taken to implement them and also to improve the water shortage? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The important issues which were stressed during the  conference are as  
follows: 
• State Governments are to ensure sustainability in drinking water  
sources both surface and ground water to prevent slippage in terms of       
quality and quantity of drinking water supply; 
• Need for effective convergence with other  govemment,programmes like  
NREGA, Water and Soil Conservation, Backward Region Grant Fund       
(RGF); 
• Dovetailing of funds with the grants provided under the XII Finance 
Commission; 
• Promotion of cost -effective technologies and revival of traditional water 
bodies and drinking water sources; Regular updation of progress on online 
monitoring system, and Improved data management for planning and 
implementation of projects. 
(c) As a follow up, the following steps have been taken to implement and  
improve the water shortage: 
• The theme document ensuring sustainability of drinking water has already 
been circulated to all the States. 
• The theme document contained several cost effective and traditional 
technologies for reviving surface water as well as under ground water 
sources. 
• Several brainstorming sessions have been held with State Governments to 
popularize these technologies.

drinking water projects. It has been circulated to the States.

ensure smoother coordination as well as effective dovetailing of funds in the 
implementation of drinking, water supply projects.

to state: 
(a) whether there is any provision in the NREG Act for State specific Rural

of guaranteed employment in a financial year to every household in the rural areas covered 
under the scheme and whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. Section 
12(1) of the Act provides for constitution of State Employment Guarantee Council by 
each State for the purposes of regular monitoring and reviewing the implementation of the 
Act.

Councils is enclosed {See below).

Annapuma Scheme in Kenda 
2422. SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the total number of beneficiaries approved under Annapooma Scheme in Kerala;  
(b) the quantity of rice required per month under the scheme; 
(c) the amount of rice presently allotted to the State under the Scheme; 
(d) whether there is a shortage in the allocation; and 
(e) if so, details thereof alongwith the steps taken to supply rice on the basis of physical 
target? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) The Annapuma Scheme was launched from 
1.4.2000 to provide food security to meet the requirement of those senior citizens who 
though eligible remained uncovered under the National Old Age Pension Scheme 
(NOAPS). Under the Annapuma Scheme, 10 Kg. of foodgrains per month are being 
provided 'free of cost' to the beneficiarj'. At the time of launch of the scheme a numerical 
ceiling was fixed for the States/UTs. The numerical ceiling for the State of Kerala was then 
fixed at 44980 which meant requirement of 450 MTs of foodgrains per month. From 2002-03, 
the scheme was transferred to the State Plan and as per the new guidelines, the State has 
been given the flexibility to implement the three schemes of National Old Age P ension 
Scheme, National Family Benefit Scheme and Annapuma by deciding the inter scheme 
allocations as per the priority accorded by the State. Hence, the Central Government releases 
combined allocation for the three schemes. 
(c) The amount of rice allotted to the State under the Scheme for 2007 -08 is 5400 
MTs. 
(d) No, Sir. 
(e) Does not arise.

Recommendations made during conference on 
rural water supply and sanitation 
2423. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister  of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether a two day annual conference on rural water supply and sanitation was 
held recently; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the details of the recommendations made and the decisions taken; and 
(d) the steps being taken by the State Government on the instructions of the Government 
to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT .(SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A two-day conference of Ministers in-
Charge of rural drinking water supply and rural sanitation in the States and the Union Territories 
was held on July 4-5, 2007 at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi. The theme of the conference was 
Sustainability in Rural Drinking Water Supply Systems and Sanitation for All. During the 
inauguration the Prime Minister released theme documents on sustainability in the rural drinking 
water supply projects and sanitation.     
(c) The important issues which were stressed during the conference are as  
follows: 
•       State Governments are to ensure sust ainability in drinking water sources 
both surface and ground water to prevent slippage in terms of quality and 
quantity of drinking water supply; 
• Need for effective convergence with other government programmes like  
NREGA, Water and Soil Conservation, Backward Region Grant Fund 
(BRGF);  
•     Dovetailing of funds with the grants provided under the XII Finance  
     Commission; 
• Promotion of cost -effective technologies and revival of traditional water 
bodies and drinking water sources; 
• Regular updation of progress on online monitoring system, and 
• Improved data management for planning and implementation of projects  
(d) The State Governments are in various stages of operationalisation of the  
recommendations of the annual State Minister's conference and follow up  action 
taken by the Department in this regard.

2424. MS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be  
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any techniques have been devised to eliminate corruption in the 
implementation of NREGA so that the benefit goes to the poor beneficiaries in rural areas;

the country during the last one year;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI

done by the Central Government on regular basis. Periodic review meetings are undertaken 
by Minister of Rural Development and Secretary (Rural Development) from time to time. 
National Level Monitors and Area officers of the Ministry visit various districts to oversee 
the progress of the Act. Comprehensive MIS has been developed that places all vital data in 
public domain. Monitoring and Vigilance Committees have been set up. Village level 
vigilance and monitoring committees have been set up for local monitoring. The Ministry is 
monitoring not only the physical parameters but qualitative indicators as well. 
(b) The basic objective of NREGA is to provide for a legal guarantee of one hundred 
days of employment in every financial year to every rural household for doing un-skilled 
manual work on demand. Para 9 of the Act provides that minimum 60% of the total cost of the 
project should be spent towards payment of wages to un-skilled labour. The focus of the Act 
is, therefore, on works which are labour intensive. A Statement indicating expenditure 
incurred on payment of wages to unskilled labourers, skilled and semi-skilled workers, on 
material and contingencies is enclosed {See below). 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Studies have been done by five independent agencies, namely, 
Indian School of Women's Studies and Development, Institute for Human Development, Centre 
for Budget and Governance Accountability, Indian Institute of Management, Banglre and 
Centre for Development Alternatives, Ahmedabad.

Pilferage of  foodgrains  under SGRY in U.P. 
2426. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether remuneration to workers employed under the Sampooma Grameen Rozgar 
Yojana is made by Government in foodgrains in lieu of cash; 
(b) if so, the State-wise details of foodgrains provided annually by Centre indicating 
its cost at respective destinations, since inception of the Yojana; 
(c) whether any investigation has been conducted into the complaint publicly made on 
30th April, 2007 by a senior member of the Cabinet accusing large scale pilferage of 
foodgrains supplied under the Yojana to the State of Uttar Pradesh and connivance of various 
levels of the State authorities therein; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and   
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) Wages are paid to workers employed under Sampooma 
Grameen Rozgar Yojana in cash and foodgrains. Para 2.2 of SGRY guidelines stipulates that 
foodgrains should be given as part of wages under the SGRY to the rural poor at the rate of 
5 kg. per manday. Should a State Government wish to give more than 5 kg. of foodgrains per 
manday, it may do so within the existing State allocation (subject to a minimum of 25% of 
the wages to be paid in cash). The State Governments and UT Administrations will be free to 
calculate the cost of foodgrains paid as part of wages, at a uniform rate which may be 
either BPL rate, or APL rate or anywhere between the two rates. The workers will be paid the 
balance of wages in cash, such that they are assured of the notified Minimum Wages. Higher 
utilization-per manday and higher price fixation offoodgrains will result in saving of cash 
component which may be utilized to meet the material cost for creation of durable 
community assets. 
In the event of non-availability/inadequate availability of foodgrains, wages in kind may 
be less than 5 kg. of foodgrains per manday and the remaining portion may be given in 
cash. In the reverse case of less availability of cash, the wages in cash may be less than 
25% and the remaining portion may be given in kind as foodgrains. However, the norm of 
minimum 5 kg. of foodgrains and minimum of 25% wages in cash should be maintained 
as far as possible. No additional allocation of cash in lieu of foodgrains will be made by 
the Central Government." 
(b) Details are given in the Statement {See below).. 
(c) to (e) The information is being collected and will be laid on the Table of the House.

States doing well under NREG Act 
2427. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) how much money has been spent on the National Rural Employment Guarantee 
Act in 2005-06; 
(b) whether it is a fact that a large amount to be spent by the Central Ministries has 
lapsed; and 
(c) the States which have performed well under this scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) NREGA was launched in 200 identified districts in the 
country on 2.2.2006. No budget provision has been made during the year 2005-06 for 
implementation of the Act. Funds had been provided to these 200 NREGA districts during 
2005-06 out of the budget allocations made under National Food for Work Programme for 
the year 2005 -06. A Statement indicating the cumulative expenditure for NFFWP and 
NREGA for the year 2005-06 is enclosed {See below). 
(b) NREGA is demand based programme and not allocation based. Funds are released to 
the districts on receipt of a proposal along with Utilisation Certificate indicating utilisation of 
at least 60% of the funds released earlier. The unutilized funds under NREGA do not lapse 
but are carried forward to the next financial year as opening balance for that year. 
(c) Performance of the States is assessed against a number of programme indicators. 
All States are responding well to the demand for employment and are able to provide 
employment. All states except Bihar, H.P., J and K, Jharkhand and Punjab have been able to

Bailing out weavers of Nagpur region from financial crisis 
†2443. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that the weavers' association of Nagpur region of Maharashtra 
have not been paid full arrears of last year under Deendayal Hathkargha Scheme so far;  
(b) if so, the reasons for non-payment of full amount; and 
(c) the efforts made by Government to bailout the weavers from financial crisis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI E.V.K.S. 
ELANGOVAN) (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. This Office had considered the claim for release 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

186   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
of Rs.2,70,45,796/ - during the last financial year received from the Government of 
Maharashtra out of which a sum of Rs.2,59,85,246/ - had been released under Marketing 
Incentive Component of DDHPY scheme. The Balance amount of Rs. 10,60,550/ - could 
not be considered because on the scrutiny of the claims in consonance with the 
governing guidelines on the subject, some of the primary handloom cooperative 
societies have computed sales figures for one year/two years only instead of three years 
which is required under the guidelines. 
(c) Yes sir. In order to bailout the weavers from financial crisis and to  meet the 
challenges of the liberalized global market, the Integrated Handloom Development 
Scheme (IHDS) has been formulated for implementation during the Eleventh Plan period 
by merging, with or without modifications of the essential components of the ers twhile 
Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana (DDHPY), Integrated Handloom Training 
Project (IHTP), Workshed -cum-housing Scheme and Integrated Handloom Cluster 
Development Scheme (IHCDS) implemented during the Tenth Plan. The objectives of 
the IHDS are to focus on formation of weavers group as a visible entity, develop the 
handloom Weavers Groups to become self -sustainable, an inclusive approach to cover 
weavers both within and outside the Co -operative fold; skill up -gradation of handloom 
weavers/workers to  produce diversified products with improved quality to meet the 
market requirements; provide suitable workplace to weavers to enable them to produce 
quality products with improved productivity; holistic and flexible intervention to provide 
need based input s specific to each cluster; market orientation by associating 
entrepreneurs and professionals for marketing, design and managing the production and 
to facilitate process of credit from financial institutions/banks. Besides, the committed 
liabilities of the  erstwhile Schemes -Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana 
(DDHPY), Integrated Handloom Training Project (IHTP), Workshed -cum-housing 
Scheme and Integrated Handloom Cluster Development Scheme (IHCDS) would also be 
met out of the overall outlay of the Integrated Handloom Development Scheme.

Programme for dalit Muslims and Christians 
†*282.   SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY:

(a) whether the Ministry has any programme for the welfare of dalit Muslims and dalit

THE MINISTER OF MINORITY AFFAIRS (SHRI A.R. ANTULAY): (a) to (c) A 
programme of affirmative action for the minorities, especially for those who are economically 
and socially backward, has already been announced. The Prime Minister's New 15 Point 
Programme for the Welfare of Minorities, launched in June, 2006, inter-alia, provides for

economic activities and employment by upgradation of skills through technical training and

schemes in this programme.

viz., a merit -cum-means scholarship scheme for technical and professional courses at 
under-graduate and post-graduate levels, a pre-matric and a post-matric scholarship scheme. 
The merit-cum-means scholarship scheme has already been approved and States/UTs 
have been advised to take further appropriate action. Besides, an exclusive coaching and 
allied scheme for minorities has been announced. The corpus of the Maulana Azad 
Education Foundation has been augmented and the equity of the National Minorities 
Development and Finance Corporation further increased in 2007 -08 to enable it to 
expand its operations and coverage. 
Advancement of education among minority communities, especially those who are 
educationally backward, is accorded high priority. A special package has been formulated for 
this purpose.

(i) Grid-interactive/distributed renewable power 
(ii) Renewable Energy for urban, industrial and commercial applications

State Governments, on the other hand , are responsible for implementation of some of

areas are the remote village electrification programmes, bio -gas, bio-mass gasifer, solar 
photovoltaic, small wind energy system and village energy security test projects in rural

Loan to power grid corporation of India Ltd. 
*292.   PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHAR TIA: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:   
(a) whether the Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. has approached the World  
Bank and the Asian Development Bank for a total loan of $ 3.2 billion, to finance  
the ambitious Rs.70,000 crore national grid project; 
(b) if so, whether any agreement with the World Bank and the Asian  
Development Bank in this regard has been worked out; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof?   
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) The 
Power Grid Corporation  of India Limited (PGCIL) has planned to raise multi -lateral 
loan assistance of about US$ 3 billion (Rs. 12,500 crore) from the World Bank (US$ 2 
billion - Rs. 8,350 crore) and Asian Development Bank (ADB) (US$ 1 billion Rs. 4150 
crore) to fund various projects during the Eleventh Plan. The loans are proposed to be 
availed in tranches. 
Out of the US$ 2 billion from the Worid Bank, first tranche of US$ 400 Million (Rs. 
1650 crore) has already become effective in Decernoer 2006. Proposal for availing 
second tranche of US$ 600 Million (Rs. 2500 crore) during 2007 is under consideration. 
The PGCIL has proposed for ADB funding of the National Grid Development 
Programme (the Investment Programme). The total programme cost is estimated at US 
$ 2,577 million out of which ADB funding is envisaged to be US $ 1 billion. The ADB 
has proposed to provide a multi -tranche sovereign guaranteed loan of US $ 800 million 
and non-sovereign loan of US $ 200 million for the following two components under 
the Investment Program - Upgradation of Transmission capacity from Uttarakhand 
(Component 1, estimated cost - US $ 383 million) and 800 kV High Voltage Direct 
Current (HVDC) Northeastern -NorthemAVesteri inter -connector (Component II, 
estimated cost - US$ 2,194 million). The sovereign  guaranteed loan (US $ 800 million) 
will be under the Multi -Tranche Financing Facility (MFF) of ADB whereby the 
Borrower tranches its requirements and the individual loans are provided by ADB to 
finance the subprojects as and when they are ready for financing and a related request is 
made through a Periodic Financing Request (PFR) under the umbrella Framework 
Financing Agreement (FFA). 
Review of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
*293. SHRIMATI N.R DURGA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a review mission, consisting of independent experts, 
reviewed the progress of the Sarva Siksha Abhiyan in the first half of 2006; 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof;   
(c) the criteria adopted in finding out the progress of SSA;  

206   Written Answers to Questions        [RAJYA SABHA] of 3rd September 
(d) whether any complaints about implementation of SSA have been received from 
States; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and the action contemplated on such complaints? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOUR CE-DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN 
SINGH): (a) to (c) The third Joint Revievi' Mission (JRM) for the Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan (SSA), reviewed the programme on the basis of visits to ten States in January, 
2006. 
The Mission's findings included an assessment that the programme is on track, that it 
has successfully reduced the number of children who were out of school by enhancing 
enrolment and retention and also that meaningful steps have been undertaken for 
improvement of quality of elementary education. 
The Mission em phasized continued focus on education of girls, children from 
educationally and socially disadvantaged sections of society and children with special 
needs; review teacher training programmes and; strengthen internal audit mechanisms. 
SSA implementation has addressed these issues, subsequently. 
(d> and (e) Recently, the School Education Department, Government of Andhra 
Pradesh has reported that an amount of Rs. 14,98,03,378/ - under District Primary 
Education Programme (DPEP)/Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) had b een diverted to 
unauthorized bank accounts by the Assistant Accounts Officer of the State Project 
Office. The State Government has taken strict action in instituting a judicial enquiry; 
undertaking investigation by the State CID and the suspension of three  accounts 
officials alongwith transfer of another three accounts personnel from the State Project 
Office. The Government of India has asked the Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India to carry out a special audit of accounts pertaining to the DPEP and SSA  for the 
period 2000-01 till date in Andhra Pradesh. 
Criteria for deemed universities 
†*294. MISS ANUSUIYA UIKEY: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the criteria fixed for obtaining the status of deemed university; 
(b) the number of autonomous colleges in the country and how many of them fulfil 
the criteria to obtain the status of deemed university; 
(c) whether the proposal to give the status of deemed university to the autonomous 
college of Chhindwara is under consideration; and 
(d) by when the decision in this regard would be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN 
SINGH): (a) The Central Government is empowered by the University Grants 
Commission (UGC) Act, 1956 to notify an institution of higher - education, other than a 
University, as Deemed to be a University, on the advice of the UGC. The UGC has laid 
down guidelines for consideration of proposals for declaring an

institution as deemed to be a university. Broadly, the guidelines of the UGC are as 
given below: 
(i)     The institutions should generally be:   
• engaged in teaching programmes and research, which are innovative, 
and of a very high academic standard; 
• capable of further enriching the University system; 
• competent to undertake application -oriented programmes in emerging 
areas of knowledge; 
• in existence for ten years or more; however, those institutions which 
impart education in the  emerging areas with promise of excellence 
can be considered for a provisional status under 
                           de-novo' category even without this condition; 
• financially sound, and also create a corpus fund as prescribed by  
the UGC; 
• recognized by the Statutory Councils like the All India Council for  
 Technical Education (AICTE), Medical Council of India (MCI), 
Dental Council of India (DCI), ,Indian Nursing Council (INC), 
Central Council of Homeopathy (CCH), etc., as the case, may be, if it 
is offering degree/diploma in professional subjects. 
(ii) Usually, institutions affiliated to universities and which are offering only 
conventional degree programmes leading to B.A./B.Com./B.Sc. or 
M.A./M. Com./M.Sc., will not be considered for grant of 'Deemed  to be 
University' status. However, such an institution, which is also offering 
innovative programmes, having adequate resources, might be considered 
for recognition as 'Deemed-to-be-University'; 
          (iii)  Institutions which are imparting routine ty pe of instruction to full -time 
students or offering training programmes for in- service personnel, unless 
of high quality, would, generally, not qualify for recognition; 
           (iv)    Outstanding  research institutions specialising  in  Social  Science s, ciences  
and Technology and conducting programmes leading to Masters and 
research degrees in specialized areas can be considered  for 'Deemed-to-be-
University' for their research  egrees and highly  specialized programmes at 
Master's level. 
(b) As per the in formation made available by the UGC, there are, presently, 272 
autonomous colleges functioning under various universities in the country. The 
suitability of autonomous colleges to qualify as 'deemed -to-be-university' can only be 
assessed on a case to case basis, as and when each autonomous college applies for 
declaration as an institution under deemed to be university category. 
(c) No, Sir.   
(d) Does not arise.

Fresh water by de-salination technology 
*295 SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of EARTH SCIENCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the extensively depicted invention of the National Institute of 
Ocean Technology, Chennai, on de-salination of sea water through Barge based plants; 
(b) in what way the technology is different from the widely patented techniques of 
de-salinating sea water; 
(c) whether it is a fact that NIOT can produce fresh water by de- salination of water 
at a cost of four paise per litre; 
(e) if so, the details thereof: 
(d) whether such costs include the capital cost of the Barge machinery and  
other fixed costs; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): The National 
Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) an autonomous body of the Mini stry has 
indigenously designed developed and demonstrated the desalination technology for 
conversion of sea water into potable water based on Low Temperature Thermal 
Desalination System (Ll ). The LTTD is a process under which the warm surface sea 
water is flash evaporated at low pressure and the vapour is condensed with cold deep sea 
water. After conducting several experiments in the Laboratory (500 Liter per day 
capacity and 5000 Liter per day capacity), a LTTD plant with a capacity of 1 lakh 
liter/day production of fresh water was developed. Considering the requirement of fresh 
water for both island territories and coastal mainland of India, two types of desalination 
Plants have been developed viz.. Land Based Plant and Barge Based plant. 
The land based p lant of 1 lakh liter per day capacity plant was installed in 
Karavaratti in May 2005. The Kavaratti plant, handed over to Lakshadweep 
Administration in April 2006 for operation and maintenance, has been effectively 
working since then and catering significantly to the needs of the population of Kavaratti. 
This LTTD plant has produced about 6 crore liter of water so far. 
A 10 -lakh liter per day capacity plant indigenously designed and developed was 
commissioned on a barge in April 2007, about 40 kms. off Chennai. The barge based 
demonstration plant was successfully had been run continuously for over a period of 
several weeks. 
(b) The LTTD technology developed by NIOT is quite different from the widely 
patented Reverse Osmosis technology in many ways. In the Re verse osmosis process, 
salts from sea water is removed using a membrane, whereas in the LTTD salts are 
removed by flash evaporating warm seawater under low pressure and condensed with 
cold seawater. There are many advantages of LTTD over reverse osmosis. T he LTTD 
technology does not require any chemica pre and post -treatment of seawater, pollution 
free, hence more suitable for island territories. The 

Written Answers to Questions [5 SEP., 2007] of 3rd September 209 
LTTD  has  less  operational  and maintena nce problems  compared  to  other 
desalination processes. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. NIOT has demonstrated production of fresh water from 
seawater "using the barge mounted desalination plant at an estimated cost per liter of 
about 6 paise per litre. The product ion cost can come down to four paise per litre in the 
long run, for higher capacity plant of IGO lakh litre per day, even though the first plant 
may cost more. 
(e) and (f) Yes, Sir., The estimated cost of production of demonstration plant is 
inclusive of capital and other fixed costs.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) Yes, Sr. 
(b) Functions and powers of the National Commission for Protection of Child 
Rights have been laid down under Section 13 and 14 respectively of the Commissions 
for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005. Relevant provisions are given in the Statement 
{See below). 
(c) Shrimati Shantha Sinha is the Chairperson of the National Commission for 
Protection of Child Rights. Two members, name ly, Shrimati Sandhya Bajaj and Ms. 
Dipa Dixit have been appointed in the Commission so far. 
(d) and (e) Appointment of the remaining four members is under process. 
Statement 
Functions and powers of the Commissions for 
Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 
Section 13 (1): The Commission shall perform all or any of the following functions, 
namely: 
(a) examine and review the safeguards provided by or under any law for the time 
being in force for the protection of child rights and recommend measures 
for their effective implementation;

(b) present to the Central Governnfent, annually and at such other intervals, as 
the Commission may deem fit, reports upon the working of those 
safeguards; 
(c) inquire into viol ation of child rights and recommend initiation of 
proceedings in such cases; 
(d) examine all factors that inhibit the enjoyment of rights of children affected 
by terrorism, communal violence, riots, natural disaster, domestic violence, 
HIV/AIDS, trafficking, m altreatment, torture and exploitation, 
pornography and prostitution and recommend appropriate remedial 
measures; 
(e) look into the matters relating to children in need of special care and 
protection including children in distress, marginalized and disadvantage d 
children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family 
and children of prisoners and recommend appropriate 
     remedial measures; 
(0 study treaties and other international instruments and undertake periodical 
review of existing poli cies, programmes, and other activities on child 
rights and make recommendations for their effective implementation in 
the best interest of children; 
(g)      undertake and promote research in the field of child rights; 
(h) spread child rights literacy amon g various sections of the society and 
promote awareness of the safeguards available for protection of these 
rights through publications, the media, seminars and other available 
means; 
(i) inspect or cause to be mspected any juvenile custodial home, or any other 
place of residence or institution meant for children, under the control of 
the Central Government or any State Government or any other authority, 
including any institution run by a social organization; where children are 
detained or lodged for the pu rpose of treatment, reformation or protection 
and take up with these authorities for remedial action, if found necessary; 
(j) inquire into complaints and take suo motu notice of matters relating to- 
(i)     deprivation and violation of child rights; 
(ii) non-implementation of laws providing for protection and development 
of children; 
(iii) non-compliance of policy decisions, guidelines or instructions aimed 
at mitigating hardships to and ensuring welfare of the children and 
to provide relief to such childre n, or take up the issues arising out of 
such matters with appropriate authorities; and

Programme of Taslima in Allahabad University 
†298. SHRI SHREEGOPA L VYAS: Will the Minister of HUMAN -RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the University of Allahabad has cancelled the 
progmmme of Taslima after the Hyderabad incident; 
(b) whether Government had given its consent; 
(c) whether some people staged a victory procession after this incident; and 
(d) if so, the views of Government on this episode? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN 
SINGH): (a) to (d) According to the information furnished by the University of 
Allahabad, the Women's Advisory Board of the University had scheduled a programme 
on 14.8.2007 in which Dr. Taslima Nasrin was to participate. However, after a review of

vitiated at the very beginning of the academic session. The University has reported that 
a few sections staged a procession, after the cancellation of the programme. 
The Government is of the opinion that the University of Allahabad is a statutory 
autonomous body established by an Act of Parliament, and it does not require any 
approval or consent of the Government for scheduling or cancelling such programmes.

(xiii) Refusal to waive state and local taxes on materials by some states.

Failure in basic education 
2150. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE  
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the reasons why we have failed miserably in providing basic education to 
millions of children, inspite of our UTs and IIMs are recognized centres of excellence;  
(b) whether it is a national disgrace; if so, whether Government are considering to 
improve the situation by providing basic education to the deprived class of millions of 
children; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof?   
THE MINISTER OF STATE  IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) Since the jnception of 
the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyah programme, in 2001- 02, there has been an increase in 
enrolment of children in 6-14 years age group in schools/alternate schooling system and 
a reduction in out of school children from 3.20 crore in 2001 to approximately 75 lakh 
in April, 2007. 
Consequent upon enactment of the Constitution (Eighty -sixth Amendment) Act, 
2002, Article 21- A has been inserted in the Constitution , which makes education a 
Fundamental Right for children in the age group of 6 -14 years by providing that "the 
State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to 
fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." Accordingly, a 
draft Model Right to Education Bill, spelling out broad parameters and features for 
achieving the constitutional mandate of free and compulsory education was drafted and 
circulated as framework to the States/UTs to seek their comments thereon.

2204. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether there has been a persistent demand from the States for enhancing 
royalty on minerals mined, commensurate with the market price of the minerals; 
(b) whether there is another long standing demand from the States to empower 
them to award mining leases, on the basis of value-addition plans in States; and 
(c) whether the proposed new mining policy would address these issues and if 
so, the details thereof?

applicants in grant of mineral concession who are willing to do value addition of 
the minerals within the State. A National Mineral Policy, which also covers this 
issue, is under consideration of the Central Government.

Test projects on village energy security in A.P. 
2220. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of NEW AND 
RENEWABLE ENERGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether test projects on village energy  security are being implemented in 
Andhra Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the aims and objectives of the projects; and 
(d) the plans of Government to extend these test projects to other parts of the 
country as they are now covering only 12 States and selected villages? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND 
RENEWABLE ENERGY (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) and (b) Three 
test projects on village energy security were sanctioned for villages in Cuddapah, 
East Godavari and Warangal districts of Andhra Pradesh as per proposals 
forwarded by the State Nodal Agency, Non -Conventional Energy Development 
Corporation of Andhra Pradesh (NEDCAP). The projects had to be cancelled 
subsequently as requested by the State Agency as these villages are being 
electrified by conventional means through grid extension. 
(c) The projects are based on utilization of locally available biomass 
resources and aim at meeting the total energy requirements including cooking, 
lighting and motive power, with full participation of the local com munities, 
including women. 
(d) A total of 200 test projects are planned to be taken up, of which 79 test 
projects are at present under implementation in 11 States. A country -wide 
programme can be considered based on the outcome of the test projects. 
Development of renewable energy sources 
2221. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
NEW AND RENEWABLE ENERGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are concentrating more on developing renewable 
sources of energy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 

Written Answers to Questions [5 SEP., 2007]           of 3rd September 289 
(c) whether it is a fact that the demand for fossil material like oil, coal and 
gas would also go up in future, leading to more pollution in the atmosphere; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND 
RENEWABLE ENERGY (SHRl VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) The Government 
is implementing a wide range of programmes for the development and 
deployment of new and of renewable energy. To encourage investment in the 
renewable energy sector, fiscal and financial incentives are being provided that 
include capital/interest subsidy, J accelerated depreciation, concessional duties 
and relief from taxes, apart from preferential tariff for grid power being given in 
most potential States. Publicity and awareness on the need and usefulness of 
renewable energy systems/devices is created through print, postal and electronic 
media and special events like the Rajiv Gandhi Akshay Urja Diwas are being 
organised. District-level Advisory Committees have also been constituted in the 
states to facilitate effective coordination of renewable energy schemes. These 
apart, research, design, and development in new and renewable energy is being 
supported. 
(b) Details of achievements under var ious renewable energy programmes as 
on 30.06.2007 are given in the Statement (See below). 
(c) and (d) The Expert Committee on Integrated Energy Policy in its Report 
(lEPR 2006) has estimated that by 2032, i.e., 25 years from now primary 
commercial energy/requi rement in the country would need to go up 4 -5 times 
the current level, electricity generation installed capacity 5.6 -7 times the current 
level and oil requirement by 3 -6 times the current level. The need to diversify 
energy supply options is brought out in  the lEPR 2006. Accordingly, increased 
focus is being laid on the deployment of renewable power that is likely to 
account for around 5 per cent in the electricity -mix by 2032. This apart, 
alternate fuels, essentially bio -fuels, are proposed to be progressi vely used for 
blending with diesel and petrol, mainly for transport applications.

among others. Environment and Forests, Agriculture, Rural  
Development, and Panchayati Raj would b e required. Further, a Biomass 
Atlas is under preparation which is expected to more accurately assess 
State-wise renewable energy potential from agro-residues. 
(2) Potential based on areas having wind power density (wpd) greater than 
200 W/m- assuming land availability in potential areas @ 1 per cent and 
requirement of wind farms ® 12 ha/MW, not all of which may be 
technically feasible for grid -interactive wind power. In line with 
international practice for setting up grid -interactive wind power systems 
on site s having wpd greater than 300 W/m -, potential would be 5000 
MW. Further, preliminary surveys do not at this juncture suggest a 
sizeable grid-interactive off-shore wind power potential. 
 (3) Technically feasible and economically viable hydro potential is ge nerally 
accepted at 40% of the total estimated potential. Accordingly, the 
technically feasible and economically viable small hydropower potential

feasible potent ial is assessed at 5000 MWe, not all of which may be 
economically viable. Furthermore, several sugar companies/ 
cooperatives are unable to develop bankable projects on account of their

(5) With expansion of urban population post census 2001, current

had been kept in abeyance on  the orders of the Supreme Court in the

2238. SHRl RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether power theft is a major impediment for the growth of power 
sector in the country; 
(b) if so, whether Government had directed the State Governments to 
launch a special drive against power theft; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

308   Written Answers to Questions    [RAJYA SABHA]         of 3rd September 
(d) whether private power companies are harassing consumers in the name 
of power theft and acting in an arbitrary manner by increasing power rates, etc. 
particularly in Delhi; 
(e) if so, the action taken so far, by Government in this regard; 
(f) whether any special courts are being set up for speedy disposal of power 
theft cases; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to 
(c) Theft of electricity is one of the majo r contributing factors impacting the 
financial health of power utilities adversely. This also contributes to poor 
quality of power supply, frequent load shedding and unscheduled outages. The 
financial health of a power utility is also one of the criteria f or assessing the 
viability of new investments. 
The reduction of technical and commercial losses is one of the critical 
components for improving distribution segment which come largely in the 
purview of the State. To enable effective control of theft of electricity, the 
Electricity Act, 2003 has incorporated specific provisions for detection of theft, 
speedy trial of theft related offences and also for the recovery of the charges of 
electricity stolen. Based on the feedback from the States and other stakehol ders, 
the Central Government has further strengthened the theft related provisions in 
the Act by enacting the Electricity (Amendment) Act, 2007. 
By this amendment in the Act, theft of electricity has been explicitly made a  
cognizable and non -bailable offen ce. The distribution licensees have been  
empowered to disconnect the supply of electricity upon detection of theft. The 
penalty for repeated theft of electricity by large consumers has also been  
enhanced.    
The Central Government has also requested the St ate Governments to take 
steps for effectively curbing power theft and has advised the introduction of 
suitable incentive schemes for informers who give clue of the source of theft of 
electricity. The reward in such a scheme is to be linked to the amount of  
recoveries that can be effected in the cases reported. The State Governments 
have also been requested to expedite setting up of special courts as provided in 
the Electricity Act, 2003 for speedy disposal of theft related cases. 
The Central Government has built a national consensus to focus on a time 
bound programme for reduction of Aggregate Technical and Commercial 
(AT&C) losses. In the Chief Ministers' Conference held under the chairmanship 
of the Prime Minister on 28th May, 2007, a unanimous resolution was adopted 
which inter alia included the commitment of the States, with appropriate 
assistance from the Centre, to establish the necessary baseline data and 
information technology applications for energy accounting and auditing, and for 
ensuring a resolute elimination of electricity theft. In the Conference, the States 
committed themselves to achieve and sustain drastic reduction in the overall 
AT&C losses in the next five years and at least to a level of 15% in the 
Accelerated Power Development and Reform s Programme (APDRP) project 
areas. 

Written Answers to Questions [5 SEP., 2007]          of 3rd September 309 
APDRP was launched in 2002 -03 under which additional central assistance 
was provided to States for taking up technical, commercial and management 
measures to reduce the losses. The technical measures included upgradation and 
strengthening of the distribution system, adoption of High Voltage Distribution 
System, Information Technology intervention, etc. Commercial measures 
included metering and billi ng and improved revenue collection. Management 
measures included adoption of energy accounting and proper network planning 
for future expansion, preparation of monitoring of the distribution system, etc.  
(d) and (e) Section 42 of Electricity Act, 2003 prov ides for establishment of a 
Forum for redressal of grievances of the consumers in accordance with the 
guidelines as may be specified by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission 
(SERC). Any consumer, who is aggrieved by non- redressal of his grievance has  
the option to represent his grievance to an authority known as Ombudsman, who 
shall settle the grievance of the consumer within such time and in such manner as 
may be specified by the State Commission. The disconnection of electricity upon 
detection of th eft is to be done only by an officer of the licensee who has been 
authorized by the Regulatory Commission. It is also mandatory to lodge a First 
Information Report (FIR) within 24 hours of detection of theft of electricity. 
Determination of power tariffs o f distribution licensees is the statutory function 
of the SERCs. In doing so SERCs are guided by the provisions contained in 
section 61 of the Electricity Act, 2003 which, inter alia, include the factors that 
would encourage competition, efficiency, econom ical use of resources, 
safeguarding of consumers interests and at the same time ensure recover}' of cost 
of electricity in a reasonable manner and the National Electricity Policy and the 
Tariff Policy. The SERC is required to determine tariff in a transpar ent way after 
hearing various stakeholders. 
(0 and (g) Section 153 of the Act empowers the State Government to 
constitute Special Courts to ensure speedy trial of the offences relating to theft of 
electricity. States of Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Chhattisgarh,  Delhi, Gujarat, 
Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, 
Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal have 
already constituted special courts for trial of electricity theft cases.

The following steps have been taken by the Government to facilitate the 
development of power projects: 
(i) With the coming into effect of the Electricity Act, 2003 the techno -
economic clearance of Central Electricity Authority (CEA) is 
no longer required for thermal generation projects. 
(ii) Concurrence of CEA is now required only for setting up of Hydro 
electric schemes whose estimated capital expenditure exceeds 
the notified limits indicated below:- 
 Rs.2500 crores, provided that:
