- The site for settmg up the hydro generatmg station has 
been allocated through the transparent process of bidding 
in a ccordance with the guidelines issued by the Central 
Government. 
 Rs. 500 crore for any other schemes not covered as stated 
above. 
(iii) The Electricity Act mandates that the Central Transmission 
Utility, State Transmission Utilities and Transmission licencees 
shall provide non- discriminatory open access to their 
transmission systems. This has provided flexibility to the 
generating companies to choose the buyers of electricity 
generated by them. 
(iv) The requirement of obtaining 'in principle' approval of the  
Planning Commission and procedure of examination by Pre 
Public Investment Board in respect of power projects has been 
dispensed with in order to reduce the time cycle of sanctioning 
of public sector projects. 
(v) A 50,000 MW hydro initiative has already been launched and the 
National Electricity Policy lays maximum emphasis on full 
development of the feasible hydro potential. 
(vi) The Tariff Policy, which was notified on 6th January, 2006 
provides that all future requirement of power should be 
procured com petitively by distribution licensees except in 
cases of expansion of existing projects or where there is a State 
controlled/owned company as an identified developer. For 
Public Sector projects, tariff of all new generation and 
transmission projects should be decided on the basis of 
competitive bidding after a period of five years or when the 
Regulatory Commission is satisfied that the situation is ripe to 
introduce such competition. 
(vii) Competitive procurement is required to be done through tariff 
based bidding which provides flexibility to supplies on internal

geological risks, simplified procedure for transfer of clearances, promoting 
joint venture arrangements etc. It also lays emphasis on increasing private 
investment in the power sector through Independent Power Producers (IPPs) 
and joint ventures. The Electricity Act, 2003 has also created conducive 
environment for investments in all segments of the industry both for public 
sector and private sector by removing barriers to entry. Subsequently, 
National Electricity Policy has also been announced by the Government in 
February, 2005. As per this Policy maximum emphasis wou ld be laid on the 
full development of the feasible hydro potential in the country. 
Keeping in view the unique problems associated with hydro projects, a 
suggestion is under examination that the exemption from tariff based bidding 
available to the public se ctor under Clause 5.1 of Tariff Policy till January, 
2011 may also be extended to the private sector.

Working of Central Electricity Authority 
  2250. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) what is the role of the Central Electricity Authority (CEA); 
(b) whether it is a fact that the CEA has failed to properly monitor the 
power projects during the Tenth Five Year Plan 
(c) whether it is also a fact that only 50 per cent of the power generati on 
target in that Plan was achieved; 
 (d) if so, to what extent CEA is responsible for not properly monitoring and 
coordinating the power projects during that Plan; and 

Written Answers to Questions [5 SEP., 2007]           of 3rd September 329 
(e) the steps proposed to wind up the Authority for its consistent failures? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) The 
Central Electricity Authority (CEA) is a statutory body, which was originally 
constituted under the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948; thereafter it has been 
continued as such under the Electricity Act, 2003. It has a large range of 
functions which have been set out in various provisions of the Electricity Act, 
2003. Some of these are as follows:- 
  preparation and notification of the Natio nal Electricity Plan with the 
approval of Central Government; 
 examination of, and concurrence to proposals for setting up hydro 
generating pfojects estimated to involve a capital expenditure exceeding 
such sum, as may be fixed by the Central Government, fr om time to 
time, by notification; 
 advise the Central Government on the matters relating to the National 
Electricity Policy, formulate short- term and perspective plans for 
development of the electricity system and coordinate the activities of the 
planning a gencies for the optimal utilization of resources to sub serve 
the interests of the national economy and to provide reliable and 
affordable electricity to all consumers; 
 specify the technical standards for construction of electrical plants, 
electric lines and connectivity to the grid; 
 specify the safety requirements for construction, operation and 
maintenance of electrical plants and electric lines; 
 specify the Grid Standards for operation and maintenance of 
transmission lines; 
 promote and assist in the time ly completion of schemes and projects for 
improving anti augmenting the electricity system; 
 collect and record the data concerning the generation, transmission, 
trading, distribution and utilization of electricity and carry out studies 
relating to cost, efficiency, competitiveness and such like matters; 
 promote research in matters affecting the generation, transmission, 
distribution and trading of electricity. 
(b) to (e) As seen from the above, the CEA as a statutory body is mandated to 
perform a number of key statutory functions, and assisting in the timely 
completion of power schemes and projects is only one of such functions. Though 
it is a fact that only about 51 % of the targeted capacity was achieved during the 
Tenth Plan, the responsibility of this ca nnot be attributed to a single organization 
i.e. CEA which in fact is not the executing agency of the projects. Delay in 
project completion occurs due to a variety of factors, including natural causes 
such as geological surprises, difficult project locatio ns etc. Furthermore, CEA is 
the key organization providing technical advice to the Government on various 
issues related to the development of the power sector. Therefore, the question of 
winding up the CEA does not arise.

International Coffee Genome Network 
2261. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the  Minister of SCIENCE AND  
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state :   
(a) whether it is a fact that India is a partner to the International Coffee 
Genome Network; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the benefits derived from it for development of markers, ESTs and  
transformation for disease resistance during the year? 

Written Answers to Questions [5 SEP., 2007]       of 3rd September  339 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL 
SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. India is one of the partner countries to the efforts  
of International Coffee Genome Network (ICGN). ICGN is a worldwide 
network of Scientists from research organizations, universities, industry within 
the coffee producing and consuming countries. The first founding meeting was 
held at Paris on 4th to 5th Ap ril, 2005 which was attended by 27 scientists from 
12 countries and 3 other International research organizations including 2 
scientists from Coffee Board and one from Centre for Cellular and Molecular 
Biology (CCMB), Hyderabad. As on today there are 49 individual members and 
5 Institutional members. The national funding for the Indian component is being 
provided by Department of Biotechnology to six institutes. 
(c) The major efforts of the ICGN concentrate on use and conservation of 
coffee genetic resources  through the application of genetic tools. A coffee 
genome database has been created by ICGN which is an open source database 
on coffee genomics and includes comprehensive information on the coffee 
specific microsatellites, ESTs, and other bioinformatic to ols. The network 
would facilitate information and resource sharing within the scientific 
community and will help breeders by providing molecular tools and know -how 
for precision breeding. The major objectives of ICGN are development of trait 
specific molec ular markers in coffee, formulation of a global and coordinated 
strategy for coffee genomics, enhancing the inter -institutional commitment to 
work jointly for value addition by avoiding repetition and to promote 
opportunities to fund common research.

Eklavya model residential schools in Rajasthan 
2280. DR. CYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the aims and the objectives of the Eklavya Model Residential Schools; 
(b) the total number of EMRS in Rajasthan, district-wise; 
(c) their teacher-pupil ratio and classroom-pupil ratio; 
(d) the achievements of the students; and 
(e) whether Government have any plan to improve the EMRS in the country, 
with particular reference to Rajasthan ? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) 
Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRSs) have been set up with the objective 
of providing quality education to Scheduled Tribes students from class VI to XII 
in different States in order to enable them to avail of higher and professional level 
educational courses as well as better job opportunities. 
(b) In the State of Rajasthan, seven EMRSs have been set up in the districts of 
Udaipur (2), Banswara (1), Dungarpur (1), Sirohi (1), Tonk (1) and Baran (1) 
Two more EMRSs have been sanctioned to the State Government of Rajasthan 
during the current financial year. 
(c) The teacher-pupil ratio is 1:30 and classroom pupil ratio is 1:50. 
(d) The State Government of Rajasthan has reported that during the academic 
session 2006 -07, average results for the class Xth board examination have been 
42.58%.     
(e) Yes, Sir. To improve the EMRSs in the country the recurring grant per 
school has already been enhanced from Rs. 30.00 lakh to Rs.72.50 lakh 
(maximum for 420 students) with effect from 1.04.2007.

Ban on illegal child adoption 
2281. SHRI B. J. PANDA: 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government propose to stop illegal child adoption to control 
human trafficking in the garb of adoption; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and        
    (c) the action plan of Government to control exploitation of children for 
pornography?    
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and 
(b) A mechanism is in existence to stop illegal child adoption. The Guidelines on 
adoption issued by the Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA) and the 
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 and its Amendment 
Act, 2006 are the available instruments for this purpose. All adoption related 
issues are governed under the above said Guidelines and provisions of the Act.  
(c) An important objective of the National Plan of Action for Children, 2005 
of the Government of India is t o protect children against sexual and physical 
abuse, pornography, etc. The provisions under Law are as follows: 
- As per Chapter XI, Para 67 of the Indian Information Technology Act, 
2000, the Government of India clearly considers online pornography is 
a punishable offence.           
- The Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 293 specifies, in clear terms, the 
sale, etc. of obscene objects to minors a punishable offence. 
- As per Section 23 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of 
Children) Act, 2000, whoever  assaults, abandons, exposes or willfully 
neglects the juvenile or   procures him to be assaulted, abandoned, 
exposes or neglected etc., shall be punishable.

Statement 
Details regarding action being taken for the empowerment of women and to 
curb crimes against them 
Law and order and other criminal matters is a State subject under the 
Constitution and therefore, the direct responsib ility for dealing with 
enforcement of the concerned Acts is that of the State Governments and the 
mechanisms under them. The registration, investigation, detection and 
prevention of crimes against women is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Govemments/UT Administrations. However, the Government of India 
has initiated a number of measures to check such crimes, such as: —  
■ Enacted the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 
2005 which provides for more effective protection of the 
Constitutional rights of women, who are victims of violence of 
any kind occurring within the family including any unlawful 
demand for dowry. 
■ Setting up of help lines for women in distress under the 
Swadhar Scheme. 
■ Support services to victims of violence through schemes s uch as 
Short Stay Homes and Swadhar under which shelter, 
maintenance, counseling, capacity building, occupational 
training, medical aid and other services are provided. 
■ Grant-in-aid schemes providing assistance for rescue and 
rehabilitation of trafficked victims as well as prevention through 
special schemes in source areas of trafficking. 
■ Redressal of grievances through interventions of National and 
State Commissions for Women. 
■ Organizing legal Literacy and Legal Awareness Cam.ps. 
■ Implementation of schemes for (i) awareness generation and 
advocacy and (ii) economic empowerment of women through 
the programmes of Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, Swayamsidha 
Project, and Support to Training and Employment Programme 
(STEP). 
■ Review of laws with a view to remove provisions which may be 
discriminatory to women and to enhance punishments for 
crimes against women. 
■ Sensitisation of judiciary and police and civil administration on 
gender issues. 
■ Follow up of reports of cases of atrocities against women 
received from various sources, including NCW, with concerned 
authorities in the Central and the State Governments. 
Apart from legislative changes in the  relevant Acts, 
instructions/guidelines have been issued to the State GovemmentsAJnion 
Territory Administrations to effectively en force legislation relating to crimes 
against women and monitor the enforcement and to give more focused 
attention to improving the administration of criminal justice system and to 
take such measures as are necessary for the 

Written Answers to Questions  [5 SEP., 2007]         of 3rd September 367 
prevention of crime against women and other vulnerable sections of society. 
The measures suggested include: 
■ sensitizing of police officials charged with the responsibility of 
protecting the women. 
■ vigorously enforce the existing legislation relating to dowry volnice  
■ set up women police cells in police stations and exclusive women 
police stations. 
■ provide institutional support to the victims of violence. 
■ provide counselling to victims of rape. 
■ take measures to elim inate trafficking in women. States have also 
been advised to constitute State Advisory Committees to advise on 
trafficking matters. 
■  ensure wider recruitment of women police officers.   
■ train police personnel in special laws dealing with atrocities against 
women. 
■ setting up of Fast Track Courts 
■ setting up of Family Courts 
■ appointment of Dowry Prohibition Officers and notification of 
Rules under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

governed by Guidelines for Adoption from India 2006 and as per the guidelines,

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE (SHRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): Sir, I am happy t o inform this august House that 
Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, GSL V -F04, has successfully 
launched our latest communication satellite, INSAT -4CR, on September 2, 2007 
from Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh. 
...(Interruptions)... 
The 2140 kg INSAT -4CR is the third satellite in INSAT -4 series. The INSAT -
4CR satellite carrying 12 high power Ku band transponders will augment INSAT 
capacity for Direct -To-Home (DTH) television and other communications 
services. 
...(Interruptions)... 
The Master Control Facility at Hassan in Karnataka acquired signals from 
INSAT-4CR soon after it entered into orbit and initial checks have indicated 
normal health of the satellite. Orbit raising manoeuvres have commenced on 
September 3, 2007 and wi ll continue during September 5 -7, 2007 followed by 
deployment of appendages, three axis stabilization, paylmid switching 'on' and in-
orbit tests. INSAT-4CR will be operationalised by end of September, 2007.
